title: LODESTAR: Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR-Inertial Odometry With Adaptive Schmidt-Kalman Filter and Data Exploitation
platform: public datasets only, 14 sequences: 2021 HILTI (5), 2022 HILTI (1), SubT-MRS (2), NTU-VIRAL (3, aerial), Newer College (3, handheld); Cavern Handheld is handheld; carriers of the HILTI and SubT-MRS Long Corridor sequences not stated
sensors: one 3D LiDAR per dataset (Livox Mid-70, PandarXT-32, VLP-16, OS1-16, or OS1-64) and IMU, with known LiDAR-IMU extrinsics
compute: Intel Core i9-13900K CPU with 32 GB RAM; 28.69 ms average computation time versus 21.04 ms for the FAST-LIO2 baseline
summary_result: LODESTAR has the lowest APE on 8 of 13 public sequences in Table V, including 1.386 m versus 3.113 m for its FAST-LIO2 baseline on SubT-MRS Long Corridor.
summary_limitation: The method handles short-term degeneracy with non-zero returns only; it fails when LiDAR returns are absent, and prolonged zero-return intervals cause IMU dead-reckoning drift.

title: ToF-Wheel Odometry: Navigating Degeneration of Localization With Limited Sensing Capabilities
platform: unnamed differential-drive robot with a forward-facing ToF camera and a Raspberry Pi 4B (self-collected); M3DGR public ground-robot sequences
sensors: forward-facing ToF camera (model not named) and differential-drive wheel encoders, no gyroscope; on M3DGR the dataset LiDAR replaces the ToF camera
compute: Raspberry Pi 4B; 12.575 ms mean and 32.902 ms P95 total per-frame update time with at most two feedback iterations
summary_result: On four self-collected stress sequences, TWO has 0.046 m mean ATE RMSE versus 0.255 m (fixed-Q) and 0.295 m (scalar-Q) ToF-wheel filters, without a gyroscope.
summary_limitation: A purely orthogonal, wheel-silent disturbance can be corrected by the ToF update but cannot trigger covariance inflation on its own, as the authors state.

title: DURAL: Degradation‐Resistant Robust Adaptive Localization by LiDAR‐Inertial‐UWB‐Wheel Fusion for Coal Mine Robots
platform: CUMT_5 coal mine robot (real tunnel); Husky in Gazebo (simulation)
sensors: Robosense 32-beam LiDAR, Xsens-G710 IMU, p440 UWB, wheel odometry (real robot); Velodyne 16-beam LiDAR in simulation
compute: Intel Core i7 industrial PC, 32 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti; 5.627 ms mean per frame on the real tunnel data
summary_result: In a real coal mine tunnel, DURAL-Full reaches 0.167 m APE inside UWB coverage and 6.525% RPE outside it, versus 0.185 m and 20.648% for DURAL-UWB.
summary_limitation: The authors state that threshold generalization, computational cost, and the effect of anchor deployment are not fully analyzed.

title: Screw-based feature constraint model and degeneracy analysis for robotic state estimation: Theory and experiments
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
platform: handheld Livox Avia rig, tracked robot with three Livox MID-360, vehicle with a 128-beam LiDAR, Livox Horizon case; SubT-MRS and heterogeneous-LiDAR public data
sensors: LiDAR (Livox Avia, Livox MID-360, 128-beam LiDAR, Livox Horizon); UWB and bearing constraints only in the theory
compute: Intel i9-10900K, 32 GB RAM; module means of about 3.85, 0.72, 0.77, and 0.45 ms per 100 ms LiDAR period
summary_result: On a helical tunnel, the IFOE residual is 0.1353 m and 0.0161 rad versus 1.7925 to 1.8331 m and 0.2059 to 0.2103 rad for three degeneracy-detection baselines.
summary_limitation: The authors exclude total divergence from scope and apply no degeneracy suppression in real tests, where drift corrupts the local feature map and causes missed and false detections.

title: An Equivariant Filter-Based State Estimator for Tightly-Coupled LiDAR–Radar–Inertial Odometry
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
platform: HeRCULES vehicle sequences (snow); SNAIL handheld, e-bike, and SUV sequences (campus, rain)
sensors: LiDAR, IMU, millimeter-wave radar (ARS548 or Oculii Eagle)
compute: Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX CPU, no GPU; 7.645 ms (ARS548) and 9.244 ms (Oculii Eagle) total per frame
summary_result: On Parking04, Eq-LRIO has 2.190 m position RMSE versus 2.493 m for FAST-LIO2; on Library03 EKF-LRIO is better (4.824 m versus 4.926 m).
summary_limitation: The authors state that the observability result is conditional on the current map being exact.

title: Tightly-coupled LiDAR-IMU-wheel odometry with an online neural kinematic model learning via factor graph optimization
platform: Rover Robotics Rover mini (four-wheel skid-steer)
sensors: Livox AVIA narrow-FOV LiDAR facing sideways, IMU, four wheel encoders; Livox MID-360 and its IMU only for training labels and reference trajectories
compute: laptop with Ryzen 9 5900HX and RTX 3060 Laptop GPU; 31 ms total per frame, about 10 ms of it online training
summary_result: On three skid-steer sequences, the method reaches 1.07, 0.25, and 0.41 m ATE versus 3.29, 0.59, and 0.99 m for the same network without online learning.
summary_limitation: The authors assume that the network is trained in feature-rich areas first and that terrain does not change drastically while entering degenerate areas.

title: Resilient odometry via hierarchical adaptation
platform: human-driven TartanDrive vehicle and a corridor vehicle (wheeled); legged robot (single 13-condition run); aerial and handheld platforms in the datasets
sensors: RGB camera, LiDAR, IMU (configuration varies by platform)
compute: not reported in the main text (no CPU or GPU model, module runtime, memory, or power)
summary_result: On eight SubT-MRS challenge sequences, Super Odometry reports 0.271 average ATE versus 0.588 for the Liu submission; the averaging weights are not stated.
summary_limitation: The authors state that performance depends heavily on accurate calibration and precise time synchronization, and that few-shot adaptation is not guaranteed for every robot.

title: MM-LINS: A Multi-Map LiDAR-Inertial System for Over-Degenerate Environments
platform: vehicle-mounted RS-LiDAR-16 rig on a campus (five sequences); handheld MID-360 rig in a factory; M2DGR, NCLT, UTBM, and UrbanLoco public sequences
sensors: LiDAR and IMU (Livox MID-360 handheld; RS-LiDAR-16 with KY-INS180-A0 IMU on the vehicle)
compute: Intel i7-9750H at 2.60 GHz; only module time fractions are reported
summary_result: On M2DGR 07-31 with injected over-degeneracy, MM-LINS reaches 0.322 m ATE versus 23.65 m for FAST-LIO2.
summary_limitation: The authors state that map fusion accuracy drops significantly when the point clouds overlap only minimally.

title: PL-VIWO: A Lightweight and Robust Point-Line Monocular Visual Inertial Wheel Odometry
venue: 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
platform: KAIST Complex Urban Dataset data vehicle (cited dataset [26]; the text refers to "vehicle speed"), 21 sequences urban18-urban38
sensors: monocular camera, IMU, and wheel encoders from the dataset; ground-truth source not described in the paper
compute: Intel Core i7 CPU (model not stated), 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA A1000 GPU; 35 ms average processing time between frames at 80% CPU (Fig. 6)
summary_result: PL-VIWO has the lowest position RMSE on 7 of 11 KAIST highway and 4 of 10 city sequences; on urban31, 191.77 m versus 334.15 m for MINS.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors; evaluation is playback of one public car dataset with loop closure and online calibration disabled, and a stereo version is future work.

title: Quantifying mobile robot localization safety for an EKF-based SLAM estimator: An integrity monitoring approach
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
platform: instrumented vehicle with a roof-rack sensor suite (Ouster-64 LiDAR and STIM-300 IMU used); simulated kinematic bicycle model
sensors: LiDAR range and bearing to landmarks and STIM-300 IMU (experiment); rear-wheel velocity, steering angle, and range and bearing to landmarks (simulation)
compute: processor and runtime not reported; truncating fault hypotheses at n_max simultaneous faults makes the cost polynomial
summary_result: In simulation, integrity risk approaches one at x = 20 m as poorly spaced landmarks enter view, while the 2σ envelope and chi-squared detector miss the association error.
summary_limitation: The method is tailored to EKF-SLAM, a chi-squared detector, and local nearest neighbors; truncating hypotheses at n_max simultaneous faults trades a looser bound for tractable computation.

title: Degradation Resilient LiDAR-Radar-Inertial Odometry
venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
platform: RMF-Owl variant flying robot
sensors: VN100 IMU (200 Hz), OS0-128 LiDAR (10 Hz), forward-facing TI IWR6843AOP-EVM radar (10 Hz)
compute: Intel i7-11800H, multithreaded, real time at 10 Hz
summary_result: In the motion-capture test, DR-LRIO has 0.242 m APE versus 0.268 m (FAST-LIO2), 0.239 m (LIO without radar), and 0.865 m (RIO without LiDAR).
summary_limitation: The authors report remaining z-drift in both the RIO and DR-LRIO solutions in the tunnel.

title: Uncertainty‐aware LiDAR‐based localization for outdoor mobile robots
platform: Agilex Hunter 2.0
sensors: Velodyne VLP-16 LiDAR, Xsens MTi-30 IMU, Emlid REACH RS+ GNSS
compute: AMD Ryzen 7 4800H laptop; 0.86 s per map-matching uncertainty query, 0.068 s per LiDAR-inertial odometry step
summary_result: Maximum 2D translation error of 0.43 m across three campus scenarios with outdated maps and dynamic traffic, while the HDL localization comparator needed reinitialization after errors above 5 m.
summary_limitation: Extended LiDAR dropouts still cause failure, and GNSS gating that assumes an accurate current pose blocks recovery after a failure.

title: FusedNet: End-to-End Mobile Robot Relocalization in Dynamic Large-Scale Scene
platform: PuduBot2 food-delivery robot with a plate-mounted Kinect v2
sensors: monocular RGB (Kinect v2 as the image source)
compute: one GeForce RTX 3080 Ti for training and inference; 38.42 ms per image
summary_result: Median real-scene relocalization error of 0.31 m and 1.07 degrees versus 0.97 m and 13.1 degrees for FeatLoc and 1.04 m and 3.09 degrees for NetVLAD, from single RGB images.
summary_limitation: Relocalization error still grows with pedestrian density, and the real scenes lack 360-degree multi-sequence coverage.

title: Visual-Inertial-Wheel Odometry With Wheel-Aided Maximum-a-Posteriori Initialization for Ground Robots
platform: unnamed wheeled robot with RealSense D455 and NVIDIA Xavier; KAIST Urban vehicle and OpenLORIS wheeled-robot datasets
sensors: monocular or stereo camera, IMU, wheel encoders
compute: Intel Core i9 3.6 GHz desktop, about 30 ms (KAIST) and 12.5 ms (OpenLORIS) per frame; NVIDIA Xavier on the authors' robot
summary_result: OpenLORIS mean initialization scale error 3.18% versus 12.84% for ORB-SLAM3; KAIST trajectory error below 0.2% of length on four sequences.
summary_limitation: Wheel slippage during initialization can yield a less accurate state, and the planar bundle adjustment assumes approximately planar ground.

title: How Safe Is Particle Filtering-Based Localization for Mobile Robots? An Integrity Monitoring Approach
platform: vehicle roof rack with Ouster 64-beam LiDAR and STIM-300 IMU; bicycle-model simulation
sensors: 64-beam Ouster LiDAR (range and bearing to landmarks), STIM-300 IMU
compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: In simulation, safety improves with landmark density until landmarks become indistinguishable; the particle filter is safer than the EKF when landmarks are poorly separated.
summary_limitation: Integrity availability is limited when the alert limit is very tight, and too-dense landmark maps raise the misassociation risk.

title: Indoor Visual Re-Localization for Long-Term Autonomous Robots Based on Object-Level Features and Semantic Relationships
platform: TurtleBot3 with Kinect V2 (IndoorVR-OC); OpenLORIS-Scene and InteriorNet datasets
sensors: RGB-D camera (Kinect V2 on TurtleBot3; OpenLORIS RGB-D cameras)
compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: Under object changes, the scene-graph method loses less Recall@5 than DBoW3 and NetVLAD; under illumination change it performs comparably; values not recorded.
summary_limitation: Featureless corridors are out of scope, and real-time operation for rigorous robotic applications is left to future work.

title: Reliable Monte Carlo localization for mobile robots
platform: Whill Model CR with Hokuyo UTM-30LX-EW
sensors: 2D LiDAR (Hokuyo UTM-30LX-EW), INS or odometry
compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: From wrong initial poses, reliable MCL relocalized faster than ROS amcl on two 2D-laser datasets and in a long-corridor building, where amcl was slow or never recovered.
summary_limitation: Failure detection follows a noisy residual classifier and cannot certify closeness to ground truth; free-space global localization is sensitive to map shape change.

title: Robust Slip-Aware Fusion for Mobile Robots State Estimation
platform: Clearpath Jackal
sensors: wheel speeds and wheel torque, IMU accelerations and yaw rate
compute: real-time implementation at 20 ms sampling; computer and runtime not reported
summary_result: Mean longitudinal-speed RMSE of 6.2% (low speed) and 8.8% (high speed) over high-grip, gravel, and slippery surfaces, with 15 tests per scenario.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors; the estimator gives proprioceptive speed and slip only, and coupling with visual-inertial navigation is future work.

title: M2DGR: A Multi-Sensor and Multi-Scenario SLAM Dataset for Ground Robots
platform: custom three-layer ground robot (unnamed chassis) with a Velodyne VLP-32C sensor suite
sensors: Velodyne VLP-32C LiDAR, fish-eye RGB cameras, RealSense D435i, thermal infrared camera, event camera, IMU, consumer GNSS; RTK/INS, Vicon, and laser tracker for ground truth
compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: On seven of 36 sequences, visual SLAM fails in darkness and no tested system tracks a lift ride; LIO-SAM reaches 1247 m ATE on Lift04.
summary_limitation: Sensors are synchronized in software, with cameras triggered through the API, and the lift and dark-room sequences remain unsolved by the evaluated systems.

title: Pose Estimation for Ground Robots: On Manifold Representation, Integration, Reparameterization, and Optimization
platform: customized campus sensor platform (ON AR0144 stereo camera, Bosch BMI 088 IMU, wheel encoders); KAIST Urban vehicles
sensors: monocular camera (left eye of a stereo pair), wheel encoders, optional IMU
compute: Intel Core i7-4790 at 2.90 GHz; optimization 9-10 ms versus 8 ms for camera-odometer fusion
summary_result: On KAIST city sequences, the second-order manifold with reparameterization and IMU gives the lowest average RMSE, 2.423 m per km, and the lowest drift on five campus sequences.
summary_limitation: Quadratic manifolds can fail on extremely uneven roads such as farmland, which a quadratic polynomial cannot model.

title: DynoSAM: Open-Source Smoothing and Mapping Framework for Dynamic SLAM
platform: none of the authors' own; KITTI tracking (car), Oxford Multimotion Dataset S4U (handheld camera), simulated Outdoor Cluster, TartanAir Shibuya, and VIODE (UAV-like motion)
sensors: stereo or RGB-D images with dense depth, dense optical flow (RAFT), and instance masks (YOLOv8); IMU only on VIODE
compute: computer not reported; front end about 100 ms per frame plus about 250 ms per object for motion refinement; full-batch back end 80-700 s, 20-frame window about 16 s
summary_result: On OMD S4U, WCME object motion error is 0.71° and 0.02 m versus 0.96° and 0.02 m for VDO-SLAM and 1.1° and 0.03 m for MVO (full batch).
summary_limitation: The authors state that full-batch optimization is computationally intensive and unsuitable for online use, and that the constant-motion model cannot capture accelerating objects accurately.

title: ProbPer-LiLo: Probabilistic Persistency Modeling for Life-Long Mapping
platform: MCD campus sequences (KTH and NTU) and the authors' MCDll extension; carriers not recorded in the legacy extraction
sensors: 3D LiDAR (Ouster 64-beam at KTH; Ouster 128-beam old and Livox Mid-360 new at NTU); point-wise semantic labels as input
compute: not reported
summary_result: On experiment E6, ProbPer-LiLo reaches 0.485 m AWD versus 1.045 m for ELite and 1.112 m for LT-mapper, with 77.40% completeness versus 33.36% and 5.47%.
summary_limitation: The authors assume that the clustering is correct and that both maps contain point-wise semantic labels.

title: Optimizing exploration with a new uncertainty framework for active SLAM systems
platform: simulated differential-drive robot in Gazebo (drive type from the text, p. 7)
sensors: simulated 360-degree 2D LiDAR (5 m range, 0.5-degree resolution); landmark-based KF SLAM
compute: not reported; only complexity orders are given
summary_result: In Gazebo, uncertainty-frontier planning lowers final SiREn dispersion, but with sigma_max 0.6 m and incomplete landmarks the map is not fully explored.
summary_limitation: The authors assume known orientation and leave a planner that combines UF and SiREn, also for non-landmark SLAM, to future work.

title: FIT-SLAM 2: Efficient 3D exploration with Fisher information and traversability-based adaptive roadmap
platform: simulated skid-steer differential-drive vehicle in Gazebo; four-wheel differential-drive rover in the field run (Fig. 17(a))
sensors: RGB-D camera with ORB-SLAM3 and VLP-16 LiDAR for traversability (simulation); ZED 2i stereo camera with ORB-SLAM3 and stereo point cloud (field)
compute: Intel i5-13420H at 3.4 GHz, ROS 2 Humble in Docker; mean planning time 20.8 ms without and 63.0 ms with Fisher information
summary_result: With simulator ground-truth poses, exploration took 880 s versus 1118 s (FAEL) in Cave and 342 s versus 479 s (GB-Planner 2) in Marsyard; tuned FAEL was faster in Corridor.
summary_limitation: The authors state that ground-truth-pose benchmarking ignores localization drift and perception errors, and that the field run was a proof of concept without benchmarking.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Autonomous Robot Exploration Using Confidence-Rich Localization and Mapping
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
platform: Turtlebot2 (Kobuki base); simulated robot in a cave map; Deutsches Museum laser dataset
sensors: 2D LiDAR (SLAMTEC A2M8), reduced to 40 beams and 8 m range on the real robot
compute: Intel i5-4210M 2.6 GHz laptop with 16 GB RAM; no per-step latency reported
summary_result: In five real Turtlebot2 office explorations per function, UCRMI needs 19.66% more time than CRMI but lowers overall uncertainty by about 32.85%.
summary_limitation: The authors state that larger environments need more particles, which raises the computational cost of weight updates and resampling and may compromise RBPF-CLAM.

title: PG-SLAM: Photorealistic and Geometry-Aware RGB-D SLAM in Dynamic Environments
platform: Bonn and TUM indoor RGB-D sequences and NeuMan outdoor sequences; carriers not recorded in the legacy extraction
sensors: RGB-D camera; Mask R-CNN segmentation and RAFT optical flow
compute: hardware model not reported; 1.93 s per frame in total; 2.3 to 2.7 GB GPU and 1.5 to 1.8 GB CPU memory
summary_result: On Bonn, PG-SLAM reaches 6.5 cm mean APE RMSE versus 12.3 cm for RoDyn-SLAM and 34.0 cm for ORB-SLAM3.
summary_limitation: The authors state that the main limitation is that the method cannot achieve real-time performance.

title: Ephemerality Meets Lidar-Based Lifelong Mapping
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
platform: LT-Parking (six sessions), MulRan DCC and KAIST, SemanticKITTI 00/01/02, MulRan 2019 and HeLiPR 2023; carriers not recorded in the legacy extraction
sensors: 3D LiDAR with per-session SC-LIO-SAM trajectories (SuMa poses for KITTI)
compute: not reported
summary_result: On MulRan DCC alignment, ELite reaches 0.942 AC, 0.111 RMSE, and 0.162 CD versus 0.738, 0.182, and 0.306 for LT-mapper.
summary_limitation: The authors evaluate the cross-session map update only qualitatively, and a threshold tailors the preservation versus update trade-off to the application.

title: NGD-SLAM: Towards Real-Time Dynamic SLAM without GPU
venue: 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
platform: public RGB-D datasets only: TUM highly dynamic sequences (4) and BONN dynamic sequences (9); carriers not described in the paper
sensors: RGB-D camera images and depth at 30 Hz (dataset sensors; camera model not named)
compute: AMD Ryzen 7 4800H laptop CPU, GPU not used; 16.72 ms mean tracking time per frame, 30.69 ms per keyframe
summary_result: On four TUM highly dynamic sequences, ATE RMSE 0.007-0.034 m versus 0.006-0.027 m for non-real-time DFS-SLAM, with 16.72 ms mean tracking time per frame on a laptop CPU.
summary_limitation: Mask propagation needs RGB-D depth, and dynamic objects outside the detector's classes, or movable objects that are currently static, are not explicitly handled.

title: JPG-SLAM: Joint Point-Gaussian Splatting Representation for Dense Dynamic SLAM
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
platform: TUM RGB-D sequences (without IMU) and OpenLORIS ground-robot sequences (with IMU, truncated to about 1000 frames); drive type not recorded in the legacy extraction
sensors: RGB-D camera and IMU; YOLACT dynamic segmentation
compute: Intel Core i7 12900K at 2.50 GHz (model as printed) with RTX 3090; tracking 239 ms per frame and mapping 2.22 s per frame on OpenLORIS Cafe
summary_result: On OpenLORIS, JPG-SLAM reaches 0.29 m mean ATE versus 0.47 m for ORB-SLAM3, 0.42 m for VINS-Mono, and 2.25 m for SplaTAM.
summary_limitation: The authors state that the system currently lacks a loop closure module.

title: Sensor-based distributionally robust control for safe robot navigation in dynamic environments
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
platform: ClearPath Jackal, described as differential-drive in the text (p. 19); Gazebo simulation
sensors: 3D LiDAR (Ouster OS1-32); 9-axis IMU (UM7)
compute: Intel i7-9700TE with 32 GB RAM onboard; CLF-DR-CBF QP at 50 Hz, A* reference path at 5 Hz
summary_result: In Gazebo with pedestrians, the CLF-DR-CBF QP reaches 93.2% success and 1.7% collision, the highest success and lowest collision of three methods.
summary_limitation: The authors state that the theory assumes valid relative-degree-1 CBFs, which can be nontrivial to find, and that evaluations use one differential-drive model.

title: FRTree Planner: Robot Navigation in Cluttered and Unknown Environments With Tree of Free Regions
platform: Unitree Go1 quadruped; simulated maze and random forest
sensors: 3D LiDAR (Livox MID360) on the real robot
compute: Intel NUC13 (i7-1360P) for the whole real system; Intel i5-13400F in simulation; no latency recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: A Unitree Go1 with a MID360 LiDAR traversed a 5 m by 6 m cluttered room with static and dynamic obstacles; simulation values are not recorded in the legacy extraction.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors; the hardware evidence is one quadruped run in a small indoor room.

title: Lifelong 3D Mapping Framework for Hand-Held & Robot-Mounted LiDAR Mapping Systems
platform: XGrids commercial handheld LiDAR mapping device; public datasets SemanticKITTI, NCLT, LT-ParkingLot, and MulRan (carriers not described in the paper)
sensors: 3D LiDAR point clouds with poses from the source mapping system (XGrids software, SC-LIO-SAM, SC-A-LOAM, or dataset poses)
compute: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X PC; about 1.5 h for dynamic removal on KITTI 00 (4500 frames); about 3 min alignment grid search for about 10 M points
summary_result: Mean F1 of 0.9488 versus 0.9278 for ERASOR over five SemanticKITTI sequences; version control stores 27 NCLT maps in 430.7 MB versus 7440.9 MB.
summary_limitation: The authors state that about 1-3% of static points remain misclassified as dynamic because not all areas are revisited during mapping.

title: LRAE: Large-Region-Aware Safe and Fast Autonomous Exploration of Ground Robots for Uneven Terrains
platform: AgileX Scout 2.0 (text: "four-wheel differential drive robot", p. 5)
sensors: Velodyne HDL-32 3D LiDAR (simulation); Livox MID360 3D LiDAR (field)
compute: Intel NUC with Core i7-1165G7 and 32 GB RAM (field); laptop with Core i7-11800H and 16 GB RAM (simulation); no timing recorded
summary_result: Up to 45.3% higher exploration efficiency and 38.8% lower travel cost than FAEL and TARE in simulation; one field run explored 954 m² in 487 s.
summary_limitation: No author-stated limitation is recorded in the legacy extraction; the field run was capped at 0.5 m/s on one bounded site.

title: Spatiotemporal Attention Enhances Lidar-Based Robot Navigation in Dynamic Environments
platform: Kobuki Turtlebot 2 (text: "differential-wheeled robot", p. 5)
sensors: Slamtec RPlidar A3 2D LiDAR (1,440 beams)
compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: In PyBullet, 86.2% success and 13.8% collisions over 1,000 episodes with two dynamic and one static pedestrian; real Turtlebot 2 tests are qualitative.
summary_limitation: The authors report slightly lower performance after the shift to iGibson; real tests are qualitative and use AMCL on a prebuilt Gmapping map.

title: Circular Accessible Depth: A Robust Traversability Representation for UGV Navigation
platform: AgileX SCOUT UGV (no drive type found in the text)
sensors: Velodyne VLP-16 3D LiDAR; WTGAHRS1 IMU and TOP103 GPS on the UGV
compute: onboard Intel i5-9400H CPU and GTX-1650 GPU, about 60 ms per frame; AMD Ryzen 7 3800X with RTX 2080 Ti for dataset timing
summary_result: In four real scenes on an AgileX SCOUT, CAD reports 100% success with zero collisions versus STVL and Autoware (Table IV), at about 60 ms per frame onboard.
summary_limitation: The authors state that binary traversability limits deployment range, that a relatively expensive LiDAR is required, and that thin structures yield inaccurate predictions.

title: Prescient Collision-Free Navigation of Mobile Robots With Iterative Multimodal Motion Prediction of Dynamic Obstacles
platform: simulated Mobile Industrial Robot MiR100 in Gazebo (no drive type found in the text)
sensors: none modeled; the occupancy grid map is given and sensor measurement is out of scope
compute: NVIDIA GTX 1650 Max-Q, about 0.3 s prediction per object; Intel i7-9750H, MPC about 0.05 s with a 0.5 s timeout
summary_result: Over 100 stochastic simulated warehouse runs, MPC-WTA* reached 95% success in scenario 1 (Table I); in Gazebo, TEB solved in 0.726 s versus 0.412 s.
summary_limitation: The authors leave physical evaluation on a robot fleet, faster prediction and MPC convergence, and handling of vision-system delay to future work.

title: Semantic OcTree Mapping and Shannon Mutual Information Computation for Robot Exploration
platform: unnamed ground wheeled robot with NVIDIA Xavier NX (indoor autonomous exploration); Clearpath Husky (outdoor joystick mapping and Unity simulation)
sensors: Hokuyo UST-10LX 2D LiDAR and Intel RealSense D435i RGB-D (indoor); Ouster OS1-32 3D LiDAR and Intel RealSense D455 (outdoor)
compute: NVIDIA Xavier NX onboard, segmentation at 9.8 FPS and OctoMap publishing every 0.34 s (indoor); onboard OctoMap update every 0.12 s (outdoor)
summary_result: On an indoor Xavier NX wheeled robot, SSMI explored an office over 20 iterations against frontier-based exploration, with segmentation at 9.8 FPS and map publishing every 0.34 s.
summary_limitation: The authors report that depth noise and classification error in the real office forced revisits and left few safe candidate trajectories; onboard compute limited the camera to 15 Hz.

title: GA-Nav: Efficient Terrain Segmentation for Robot Navigation in Unstructured Outdoor Environments
platform: Clearpath Jackal and Clearpath Husky (no drive type found in the text)
sensors: Intel RealSense RGB camera (70-degree field of view); Velodyne 3D LiDAR for localization and elevation map
compute: Alienware laptop (Intel i9, NVIDIA RTX 2080) mounted on the robot
summary_result: Average mIoU gains of 13.47% on RUGD and 10.54% on RELLIS-3D; on Jackal and Husky, off-road success 71% versus 62% for TERP (Table V).
summary_limitation: The authors state that the work focuses on perception, that labels must be correct and consistent, and that drastic elevation changes and extreme weather remain open.

title: A Sim-to-Real Pipeline for Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Robot Navigation in Cluttered Rough Terrain
platform: Jaguar 4x4 (text: "skid-steered mobile robot", p. 5)
sensors: Velodyne VLP-16 3D LiDAR; Stereo Labs ZED Mini stereo camera with IMU
compute: DRL policy on a desktop server (Intel i7-7700K) over Wi-Fi; onboard Intel NUC i5 for elevation mapping and control; Jetson TX2 for ZED pose
summary_result: A Jaguar 4x4 navigated point to point over a lab pallet-and-ramp course, with higher success and lower travel distance and time than a classical and a deep-learning comparator.
summary_limitation: The authors state that DRL can overfit the training terrain and generalize poorly to dissimilar terrain; sim-to-real map deviation caused failed real trials.

title: Visual SLAM for robot navigation in healthcare facility
platform: unnamed hospital mapping robot with Microsoft Kinect RGB-D (chassis and drive type not given in the text found); TUM RGB-D dataset
sensors: Microsoft Kinect RGB-D camera

summary_limitation: The authors plan to improve real-time performance and report that Mask R-CNN results are inaccurate around object contours.

title: A Lifelong Learning Approach to Mobile Robot Navigation
platform: Clearpath Jackal (text: "four-wheeled differential-drive unmanned ground vehicle", p. 4)

summary_result: Over 60 physical trials in three static indoor environments, LLfN reduced traversal time and recoveries versus DWA and avoided the forgetting of sequential training (Table I).
summary_limitation: The authors state that LLfN fails to learn when the base policy is incompetent everywhere, and leave dynamic obstacles and experience prioritization to future work.

title: Vehicle-Cloud Cooperative Trajectory Planning via Switched Model Predictive Control for UGVs in Unstructured Transportation Environment
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
platform: small-scale Ackermann UGV in a 3 m by 3 m test site (drive type from the text, p. 10); Gazebo/ROS vehicle model in simulation

summary_limitation: The authors place wireless timeouts and dropouts outside the operational design domain; round-trip latency above 0.2 s triggers a fail-safe stop.

title: Seeing Danger Before Moving: Learning Environment-Centric Risk for Safe Robot Navigation
platform: custom rover with a 3D-printed chassis (wheels visible in Fig. 3, p. 7; drive type not reported)
sensors: environment-mounted OAK-D Pro RGB-D cameras and seven hazard sensor types; onboard sensing only for localization and motion

summary_result: In a three-corridor physical hazard testbed, EnvGuard reaches success 0.95 with 12.8 s exposure versus 0.90 and 19.8 s for unfiltered probabilistic risk.
summary_limitation: The authors assume calibrated, sufficiently covering infrastructure sensors and reliable communication, do not model fast-moving people or robots, and fix the transition parameters.

title: A Unified Framework for Mission-Gain-Aware Proactive Planning and Control of Autonomous Mobile Robots
platform: Husarion ROSbot with Bitcraze Crazyflie scout (occlusion); Clearpath Jackal with UFactory Lite6 arm (vibration)

compute: not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: Over loose debris, the payload stayed intact in 19 of 20 mission-gain runs versus 2 of 20 full-speed baseline runs, with peak acceleration falling from about 4.19 g.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors in the legacy extraction; lab pose came from Vicon, and the occlusion simulations ignored physical collisions.

title: Circulation-embedded Control Barrier Function for safe navigation: A solution to avoid undesired equilibria and dysfunctional circulation
platform: TurtleBot3 Burger (one robot; four robots in the deadlock test)
sensors: 2D LiDAR (360 samples, 5 Hz, range set to 0.5 m); Vicon motion capture for robot position
compute: remote Intel i7 PC over Wi-Fi and ROS; 0.02 s step; mean 0.485 ms per step for parameters and QP solve
summary_result: One TurtleBot3 run passed a nonconvex obstacle with circulation held from about 9 s to 46 s, while the no-hold variant stayed trapped; mean filter runtime 0.485 ms.
summary_limitation: Feasibility under other system dynamics or added constraints is beyond the paper's scope, and extending circulation to 3D is stated to be challenging.

title: Dynamic Movement Primitives With Control Barrier Functions for Constrained Trajectory Planning
platform: custom-built mobile robot with a ROS2 interface (drive type not recorded in the legacy extraction)
sensors: not reported (the legacy card found no localization or obstacle sensor model)
compute: closed-form CBF correction; no processor or solve time reported
summary_result: In a narrow-corridor simulation with two moving obstacles, CMP stays at 0.015 m RMSE from the reference versus 1.304 m for a potential-field DMP.
summary_limitation: The closed-form safe input holds for a single CBF; combining CBFs, uncertainty, unpredictable dynamic obstacles, and 3D motion are left to future research.

title: Scenario-based motion planning with bounded probability of collision
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
platform: Clearpath Jackal (hardware); simulated unicycle robot; simulated car in CARLA
sensors: motion capture for robot and pedestrian positions; EKF for pedestrian velocity
compute: Intel i9 CPU at 2.4 GHz in simulation; SH-MPC 27 ms mean (66 ms maximum) at 20 Hz with eight pedestrians; hardware computer not reported
summary_result: In eight-pedestrian Gaussian simulation, SH-MPC finished in 16.0 s versus 18.4 s (CC-MPC) and 19.2 s (S-MPCC) at equal joint-risk specification, with maximum joint CP 0.0092 against 0.05.
summary_limitation: The guarantees rely on an accurate uncertainty model, and real-time performance is tied to 2D environments with disc-shaped collision regions and a support limit estimated online.

title: Safe Navigation in Uncertain Crowded Environments Using Risk Adaptive CVaR Barrier Functions
venue: 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
platform: simulated double-integrator robot in a 12 m by 12 m crowd simulator (no wheeled model; p. 6)
sensors: simulated 5 m sensing range; no physical sensor
compute: not reported; Delta t = 0.1 s is the simulation step
summary_result: With 5 obstacles and sigma 0.05 in simulation, the risk-adaptive CVaR-BF reaches success 0.917 and collision 0.058 versus CrowdNav++ 0.833 and 0.167.
summary_limitation: The authors note that no solution may exist under the maximum risk level in dynamic scenes, and leave prediction-error quantification and realistic validation to future work.

title: Robust Control Barrier Functions Using Uncertainty Estimation With Application to Mobile Robots
platform: tracked mobile robot on a 25-degree slope with carpet patches (text and Fig. 3, p. 7); simulated elastic actuator
sensors: full-state measurement or estimate assumed; hardware sensing described in reference [31], not in this paper
compute: 50 Hz control loop on the robot; onboard computer described in reference [31]; QP solve time not reported
summary_result: On a 25-degree slope with slip, the uncertainty-estimating CBF-QP keeps the tracked robot inside the safe set, whereas the nominal CBF-QP leaves it.
summary_limitation: The bound delta_L is set beforehand; the authors leave its data-driven estimation and state estimation errors to future work.

title: Differential High Order Control Barrier Function-Based Safe Reinforcement Learning
platform: kinematic model [x, y, v, theta] of a wheeled mobile robot (text, p. 6); no physical robot
sensors: model states and obstacle positions; no perception
compute: penalty network of two 256-unit ReLU layers; no hardware, training time, or QP time reported
summary_result: In numerical navigation tests, learned HOCBF penalties reach rewards near the alpha = 8 setting and keep the QP feasible where fixed alpha = 8 becomes infeasible.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors; the evidence is numerical tests of a wheeled kinematic model with one or three obstacles.

title: Leveraging motion perceptibility and deep reinforcement learning for visual control of nonholonomic mobile robots
platform: Robotnik Summit-XL, four-wheeled nonholonomic robot (text, p. 10; drive type not stated); PyBullet training twin
sensors: front RGB camera for control; embedded 3D LiDAR with DLO only for evaluation
compute: training on RTX 3090 and i9-12900KF; onboard RTX 2080 Ti inference about 3 ms, about 2 GB
summary_result: Zero-shot on a real Summit-XL in an indoor poster room, the recurrent PPO visual-servoing policy converges with mean errors of about 0.20 m and 7.9 degrees.
summary_limitation: The authors state that DRL needs simulator training, a deployment bottleneck versus plug-and-play classical visual servoing, and that ground friction lowers real convergence precision.

title: Mobile Robot Collision Avoidance Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning With Motion Constraints
platform: TurtleBot2 with Kobuki base, NUC12, and D435i (text, p. 9); Unity ML-Agents training and Gazebo validation
sensors: onboard RealSense D435i depth for the policy; IMU and wheel odometry fused by robot_pose_ekf for pose

summary_result: The depth-only PPO-LSTM policy is compared with DWA, TEB, and DRL_VO on 50 BARN maps in Gazebo at 0.5 and 1.0 m/s; the legacy card records no values.
summary_limitation: The authors identify localization accuracy and rapid perception of moving objects as limitations after the real-world trials.

title: NAMR-RRT: Neural Adaptive Motion Planning for Mobile Robots in Dynamic Environments
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
platform: unnamed 0.45 m x 0.45 m x 1.23 m wheeled robot
sensors: Ouster OS0-32 LiDAR, Intel RealSense D435i

summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors; evidence is three simulated maps with dataset pedestrian trajectories plus indoor trials with moving obstacles on one unnamed robot.

title: Constrained Predictive Learning Control for Omnidirectional Wheeled Mobile Robots via Reducing Iteration Horizon
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
platform: custom four-Mecanum-wheel omnidirectional robot (STM32F407, Jetson Nano, UWB positioning)

summary_result: After 9 learning iterations on the Mecanum robot, tracking errors stayed below 0.07 m and 0.03 rad; the reducing horizon cut offline solve time from 692.95 s to 277.23 s.
summary_limitation: The lifted-model optimization is computationally heavy, so the controller suits moderate-length trajectories, and initial-condition assumptions restrict its application.

title: Real-Time Multilevel Terrain-Aware Path Planning for Ground Mobile Robots in Large-Scale Rough Terrains
platform: articulated tracked search-and-rescue robot with flippers; differential-wheeled robot in Gazebo only
sensors: LiDAR, IMU (FAST-LIO2 pose)
compute: Intel Core i9-10900K CPU, 32 GB RAM, onboard; runtimes not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: In simulation and field tests over map volumes up to 1360 m3, the planner outperformed ECTN, PUTN, SSSN, CS, and GEO; the legacy extraction records no values.
summary_limitation: Terrain-material and friction prediction is out of scope under a quasi-static assumption, and real configuration errors exceed simulated ones because of localization and mapping uncertainty.

title: Adaptive High-Order Control Barrier Function-Based Iterative LQR for Real Time Safety-Critical Motion Planning
platform: wheeled mobile robot with a UWB positioning system (drive type not recorded in the legacy extraction)
sensors: ultra-wideband positioning system for robot and obstacle poses (up to 50 Hz)
compute: Intel i5-12400 PC, Python qpsolvers; HOCBF-ILQR inputs within the 0.05 s sampling period
summary_result: On a UWB-localized wheeled robot, HOCBF-ILQR computes each control input within the 0.05 s sampling period, while RB-ILQR needs at least 0.62 s in simulation.
summary_limitation: The robot model is assumed known; the authors leave model uncertainty in real-time motion planning to future work.

title: LiDAR-Based Online Control Barrier Function Synthesis for Safe Navigation in Unknown Environments
platform: three TurtleBot3 Burger robots
sensors: 2D LiDAR (360 beams at 1 degree, 5 Hz, 1 m range used); robot pose from Vicon
compute: remote Intel i7 PC; GP plus QP 7.96 ms mean, 21.11 ms maximum per step
summary_result: In one run of three TurtleBot3 Burgers at 0.15 m/s, the GP-CBF filter avoided static and dynamic obstacles; GP plus QP took 7.96 ms mean, 21.11 ms maximum.
summary_limitation: QP feasibility relies on unconstrained inputs (input constraints may make it infeasible); safety across data updates needs a fast update rate; LiDAR anomaly detection is out of scope.

title: Relaxing the Limitations of the Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance Algorithm for Mobile Robots in Crowds
platform: unnamed wheeled mobile robot with Intel RealSense D435i
sensors: Intel RealSense D435i RGB-D camera (pedestrian tracking and speed estimation)
compute: training on i7-8700 with GTX 1070; real runs on a laptop with i7-10875H and RTX 2070; timing not recorded in the legacy extraction
summary_result: In Gazebo crowds of 8 and 20 pedestrians over 1000 test cases, the method reduced collision probability and ORCA no-solution counts against ORCA baselines; the legacy extraction records no values.
summary_limitation: No limitation is stated by the authors in the legacy extraction; real crowd tests are short indoor encounters and the mobile base is not named.

title: Path Generation for Wheeled Robots Autonomous Navigation on Vegetated Terrain
platform: four-wheel differential-drive robot (text: "A four-wheel differential-drive mobile robot", p. 6)
sensors: RS-Helios 5515 32-beam LiDAR, IMU (camera only for video)
compute: two Intel NUC i5 2.4 GHz, 16 GB (planner and SLAM separately); global plan 2 Hz, local NMPC 10 Hz
summary_result: In outdoor vegetated trials, PE-RRT* produced shorter paths with larger safety distance than PF-RRT* and RRT*+PrevMap, while Pro-RRT* collided; the legacy extraction records no values.
summary_limitation: The squared-exponential kernel assumes smooth, continuous ground and vegetation, so support-plane accuracy drops on steeper terrain or more complex vegetation.

title: Remote UGV Control via Practical Wireless Channels: A Model Predictive Control Approach
platform: simulated UGV modeled as unicycle kinematics (radius 0.34 m, 1 m/s, 140 deg/s); no physical robot
sensors: simulated range-bearing beacon at the origin (Gaussian noise); no onboard sensor
compute: multi-core MPC time per step 32.47 ms (Exp. 1) and 33.92 ms (Exp. 2) at a 10 ms sampling time; processor and solver not reported
summary_result: In numerical circle and eight-curve tracking with packet loss and delay, Euclidean error averaged 22.38 and 13.48 cm, versus at least 24.54 and 22.99 cm for three baselines.
summary_limitation: The authors model only quasi-static Rayleigh fading and note the UGV may not keep the safety margin from all obstacles once localization accuracy degrades.

title: Learning‐based model predictive control for improved mobile robot path following using Gaussian processes and feedback linearization
platform: Clearpath Husky A200 (text: "skid-steer mobile robot", p. 3)
sensors: Swift Navigation Duro RTK GPS, LORD 3DM-GX5-25 IMU; wheel speeds used in analysis
compute: Dell XPS 15 laptop (i7-7700HQ, 12 GB), ROS Kinetic, Python 2.7; 10 Hz control
summary_result: On an infinite-shaped sand path, GP-FBLMPC reduced lateral and heading path-following errors by 85.31% and 59.2% versus FBLMPC, matching GP-NMPC at lower compute.
summary_limitation: Offline GP estimation on a full disturbance data set limits use in new unknown environments, and GP uncertainty is not propagated, so predictions can be overconfident.

title: Deep reinforcement learning based mobile robot navigation: A review
platform: none (literature review)
sensors: not applicable (reviewed work uses 2D and 3D LiDAR, RGB, and RGB-D cameras)
compute: not applicable (literature review)
summary_result: Literature review that organizes DRL navigation into four scenarios (local obstacle avoidance, indoor, multi-robot, social navigation); it reports no new experiments.
summary_limitation: DRL navigation converges poorly when the policy space is too large, so agents are trained in specific scenes; deployment usually needs the training sensors.

title: Sliding mode control for trajectory tracking of nonholonomic wheeled mobile robots
venue: IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation
platform: MIRO robot-soccer robot, 7.5 cm cube (text: "two driving wheels and one passive centered orientable wheel", p. 7)
sensors: overhead TMC-7 CCD camera (320x240, 30 Hz) for pose
compute: Pentium-133 host sends RF commands at 9600 bps; 33 ms sampling period
summary_result: On a MiroSot pitch, the sliding-mode tracker followed straight and curved references from small and large initial errors, while Bloch-Drakunov tracking failed to converge in Y.
summary_limitation: The robot heading must not be tangent to any circle around the world origin, which restricts feasible paths; robust control under model uncertainty remains open.

title: WiSER-X: Wireless Signal-Based Decentralized Multi-Robot Exploration Without Explicit Information Exchange
platform: two modified TurtleBots (70 m2 test); two or three robots in the larger-space test; three simulated ground robots in Gazebo
sensors: 2D LiDAR (GMapping), Qorvo DWM1001-DEV UWB ranging, rotating dual-antenna Wi-Fi (WSR) angle-of-arrival
compute: UP-Squared boards onboard for sensing, measurement generation, and SLAM; WiSER-X decisions run offboard in real time; no CPU load reported
summary_result: In 20 Gazebo runs per condition, WiSER-X has 58% less coverage overlap than an independent-frontier baseline and 23% more than a full-information-sharing baseline.
summary_limitation: The authors assume known environment boundaries and known initial global robot positions, and leave intermittent communication to future work.

title: 4CNet: A Diffusion Approach to Map Prediction for Decentralized Multirobot Exploration
platform: Clearpath Jackal (two outdoors, two indoors) and one Clearpath Ridgeback indoors; three simulated Jackals in Gazebo
sensors: 360-degree Velodyne LiDAR, wheel encoders, IMU, GPS; RTAB-Map mapping
compute: GTX 1050 GPU on the robots for map prediction (latency not reported); 5.452 s per prediction on an RTX 4090
summary_result: In 30 x 30 m simulation with a high energy budget, 4CNet-E covers 58% of the area versus 42% (NPE), 42% (AEM), and 43% (T-AEM).
summary_limitation: The authors assume that each robot obtains its position in a global frame from onboard GPS.

title: Multi-Robot Collaborative SLAM (Multi-SLAM) With Distributed Lightweight Predictive Frontier Exploration (LPFE)
platform: mini four-wheel skid-steer robots (4 in a 160 m2 office, 8 in a 1300 m2 corridor); Gazebo robots in simulation
sensors: RPLiDAR A3M1 (hardware); simulated 10 m, 180-degree laser
compute: LattePanda Alpha with Core m3-7Y30 and 8 GB onboard; simulation on i9-12900H, 64 GB, RTX 3070 Ti; LPFE plans at 0.3 Hz
summary_result: In simulation, LPFE with Multi-SLAM explores on average 1.7 and 1.4 times faster than RRT and MMPF, with 65% and 38% less overlap.
summary_limitation: The authors state that deterministic peer inference degrades gradually with longer disconnections and only maintains coordination in short outages.

title: DMT-CPP: A Delaunay-Graph-Based Framework for Real-Time Multi-Robot Online Target Coverage
platform: two TurtleBot3 Burger (2.25 x 2 m) and three TurtleBot4 (5.5 x 4.4 m); simulated robots at 1 m/s
sensors: OptiTrack motion capture for localization; occupancy cells within 1 m of each robot sent to the planner (sensor not named)
compute: simulation on i7-10700F; 24.54 ms per coverage step (15 robots, 100 targets, Map 1); hardware planner computer not reported
summary_result: With 100 targets, DMT-CPP cuts coverage completion time by up to 27.10% and 11.31% versus MAC-Planner and ACO-VP in simulation.
summary_limitation: The authors treat the allocation behavior as a principled heuristic rather than a strict theoretical guarantee; the planner is a centralized entity.

title: Commerge: Communication-efficient, robust, and fast LiDAR map merging framework for multi-robot coordination in resource-constrained scenarios
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
platform: unnamed four-wheel robots (INHA-Indoor, INHA-Outdoor), custom rover (INHA-Cave), legged robot (INHA-Planetary); public HeLiPR, Kimera-Multi, WildPlaces, MCD, and Botanic Garden data
sensors: 3D LiDAR (spinning Ouster and Velodyne, non-repetitive Livox) with FAST-LIO2 LiDAR-inertial odometry; robots send SOLiD descriptors and keyframe poses
compute: central server on Intel i7-12700KF (32 GB), IPC-6000 with i5-8265U (8 GB), or Jetson Nano (4 GB); 17.122 s communication time on Town 01-03 (IPC-6000)
summary_result: On HeLiPR Town pairs, Commerge exchanged 13.7 MB on average versus 14.8 GB for full-scan baselines and 43.3 MB for KISS-Matcher, with 5.619 m versus 6.412 m merging RMSE.
summary_limitation: A central server is required; on large HeLiPR sequences real-time merging remains challenging on IPC-6000 and Jetson Nano, and decentralization is future work.

title: Parallel Graph Inference for Decentralized and Asynchronous Multi-Robot Cooperative Localization Under Limited Connectivity
platform: five ground robots of the public UTIAS dataset (three beacons, two clients); simulated underwater robots in Webots
sensors: UTIAS: odometry (forward speed, yaw rate) and camera range and bearing; simulation: IMU, compass, depth, forward-looking sonar, USBL on 10% of robots
compute: i7-10750H offline; one-step inference 11.5 ms (simulation) and 6.9 ms (UTIAS)
summary_result: One-step inference takes 11.5 ms (simulation) and 6.9 ms (UTIAS) versus 81.1 and 46.9 ms for windowed GBP with window 10, on an i7-10750H offline.
summary_limitation: The authors note that outdated mutual measurements contribute negligibly at long delays; at 8 s delay, accuracy approaches dead reckoning.

title: Predefined-Time Fault-Tolerant Formation Control for Large-Scale Heterogeneous Wheeled Mobile Robot Swarms
platform: Six numerical heterogeneous wheeled mobile robots (two-wheeled agents 1-3, three-wheeled agents 4-6) and a virtual leader; drive type not reported
sensors: None stated (numerical rigid-body models)
compute: Not reported
summary_result: In numerical simulation of six faulty heterogeneous robots, tracking errors enter a neighborhood of zero before the predefined time of 25 s, with smaller overshoot than FT-FTFC.
summary_limitation: The authors leave directed and switching topologies and air-ground swarms to future work; evidence is theory plus numerical simulation on an undirected graph.

title: SlideSLAM: Sparse, Lightweight, Decentralized Metric-Semantic SLAM for Multirobot Navigation
platform: three Scarab UGVs (closed-loop runs); Falcon 250 UAV and Falcon 4 UAV (recorded, hand-carried or manually piloted runs); SemanticKITTI
sensors: RGB-D camera (RealSense D435i or D455) with YOLOv8 or YOLO-World, or 3D LiDAR (Ouster OS1-64) with RangeNet++; VIO or LIO relative odometry; IMU roll and pitch
compute: onboard Intel i7-10710U (Falcon UAVs) and i7-8700K (Scarab); replay on a laptop i7-10750H without GPU, graph optimization 2.4-4.0 ms indoor and 36.46 ms forest
summary_result: SlideMatch versus SlideGraph mean inter-robot position error: 0.28 versus 0.75 m for three indoor Scarab pairs, 0.13 versus 0.24 m for six replayed LiDAR UAV pairs.
summary_limitation: Objects are modeled by three primitive shapes; one-shot inlier-threshold loop closure can fail in repetitive layouts, and dynamic objects are not modeled and can cause faulty loop closures.

title: Multi-robot rendezvous in communication-restricted unknown environments via backtracking and semantic frontier-based exploration
platform: simulated TurtleBot3 Burger robots in Gazebo (teams of 3, 5, and 8)
sensors: simulated 10 m 2D LiDAR; Gmapping; semantic regions from an oracle
compute: not reported (processor, memory, GPU, and per-step time not given)
summary_result: With three robots on three maps, FBE-BT-U(0.5) reduces mean rendezvous time by 43.35% versus FBE, at 6.89% less jointly explored area, in Gazebo simulation.
summary_limitation: The authors leave empirical evaluation on real multi-robot systems to future work; all results are Gazebo simulations with an oracle for semantic regions.

title: Riemannian Optimization for Active Mapping With Robot Teams
platform: Two ClearPath Jackal UGVs and one F1/10 car (hardware); six ClearPath Husky robots in Unity and four Jackals in Gazebo; drive type of the Jackal from the vocabulary example, not from the paper text
sensors: RGB-D camera (RealSense D455); 3D LiDAR (Ouster OS1-32) on the Jackals; 2D LiDAR (Hokuyo UST-10LX) on the F1/10 car

summary_result: No numeric team result is recorded in the legacy extraction; onboard distributed semantic mapping ran at about 2.1-2.6 Hz on two Jackals and an F1/10 car.
summary_limitation: The authors state that Theorem 1 guarantees only a locally optimal consensus solution, and that extended communication interruptions could make robots revisit explored areas.

title: Communication-Constrained Multi-Robot Exploration with Intermittent Rendezvous
venue: 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
platform: four simulated robots in Gazebo and ROS (drive type not recorded); discrete grid agents in the benchmark
sensors: Gazebo: 360-degree LiDAR for gmapping, four RGB cameras for short-range dynamic obstacle avoidance; benchmark: 5-cell field of view
compute: not reported (no CPU or GPU, genetic-algorithm solve time, or planning period)
summary_result: In the discrete London benchmark, OursSync completes exploration in 6996 +/- 116 steps versus 11818 +/- 1354 (base station) and 10558 +/- 827 (two relays per robot).
summary_limitation: The authors note that rendezvous events still need a synchronization protocol and that replanning needs common information; all evidence is simulated.

title: iMESA: Incremental Distributed Optimization for Collaborative Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
platform: carriers not named in the paper; public Nebula Autonomy multi-robot LiDAR pose graphs (LAMP 2.0) and synthetic 2D and 3D factor graphs
sensors: back-end inputs only: odometry and inter-robot relative-pose, bearing+range, or range factors (synthetic); LiDAR-derived LAMP 2.0 pose graphs (Nebula)
compute: GTSAM iSAM2 per robot; average iteration below 0.04 s at 10k poses, computation only, network time excluded; processor not reported
summary_result: On four Nebula datasets replayed with simulated 100 m pairwise communication, iMESA's summed translational iATE was 1.46/1.20/0.65/3.14 m versus 1.48/1.20/0.53/3.05 m for centralized iSAM2.
summary_limitation: The authors state that iMESA is sensitive to outliers, needs every started two-stage exchange to finish, has no convergence guarantee, and onboard field operation is future work.

title: CURE: A Hierarchical Framework for Multi-Robot Autonomous Exploration Inspired by Centroids of Unknown Regions
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
platform: Three Pioneer3-DX robots (hardware); Kobuki bases in Gazebo, described with two-wheel differential-drive limits in the legacy extraction
sensors: 2D laser scanner; wheel odometry (Gmapping)
compute: One laptop per Pioneer3-DX; simulation on an Intel Core i7-11800H laptop; centroid detection under 10 ms
summary_result: Versus the RRT-based MR-RBE explorer, CURE reduces exploration time by up to 50.7% and path cost by up to 34.4% in Gazebo simulation.
summary_limitation: The authors state that the centralized architecture makes central-node data transmission grow sharply with team size and leave a distributed version to future work.

title: Communication-Efficient Multi-Robot Exploration Using Coverage-Biased Distributed Q-Learning
platform: TurtleBot3 in ROS Gazebo; real TurtleBot3 runs shown only in a video
sensors: 2D laser scanner (15 m range in simulation); wheel odometry (Gmapping)
compute: Not reported beyond CPU and RAM usage per method in Gazebo
summary_result: In Gazebo with TurtleBot3 teams, CQLite reached the same mapping efficiency as RRT and DRL explorers with about half the CPU load and 80% less communication.
summary_limitation: The authors leave reward generality to other multi-robot tasks to future work and assume flat ground and a connected communication graph.

title: Robust Task Scheduling for Heterogeneous Robot Teams Under Capability Uncertainty
platform: Simulated heterogeneous agents (ground vehicles, quadcopters, service robots in the pandemic case; capture-the-flag game agents); no physical robot
sensors: None (agent capabilities are modeled as random vectors)
compute: Intel i7-7660U laptop with Gurobi; mean assignment time 0.04 s for CTAS versus 0.43 s for STRATA in capture-the-flag
summary_result: In capture-the-flag simulation, CTAS wins more often than STRATA and needs 0.04 s versus 0.43 s per assignment; pandemic missions scale to 140 agents and 40 tasks.
summary_limitation: The authors leave a distributed planner for communication constraints and agent loss, and online plan updates, to future work; plans are fixed before the mission.

title: MR-TopoMap: Multi-Robot Exploration Based on Topological Map in Communication Restricted Environment
platform: Real wheeled robots with RPLIDAR A1, three RGB cameras, and Jetson Xavier NX (chassis not named; Fig. 8(c)); TurtleBot Burger in Gazebo
sensors: 2D LiDAR (RPLIDAR A1 on hardware; 360° laser with 7 m range in simulation); panoramic RGB (three 120° cameras on hardware, four 90° cameras in simulation)
compute: NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX onboard; timing not recorded
summary_result: Versus occupancy-grid sharing schemes, topological-map sharing cuts communication traffic by 84%-90% and raises exploration efficiency by 23%-77% in Gazebo and real-robot tests.
summary_limitation: The authors state that map building and merging rely heavily on the image-retrieval threshold; exploration fails at 0.65 and map merging fails at 1.

title: Reinforcement Learned Distributed Multi-Robot Navigation With Reciprocal Velocity Obstacle Shaped Rewards
platform: Up to eight Turtlebots, described as differential-drive in the text (p. 7); disc robots in OpenAI Gym
sensors: Neighbor positions and velocities within 4 m (RVO and VO vectors); UWB localization and ROS messaging on hardware

summary_result: On 4, 6, and 8 real Turtlebots in a circle crossing, RL-RVO reaches 1.00, 0.91, and 0.89 success versus 1.00, 0.85, and 0.68 for NH-ORCA over 50 trials.
summary_limitation: The authors leave navigation under more challenging real-world uncertainties to future work.

title: SysNav: Multi-Level Systematic Cooperation Enables Real-World, Cross-Embodiment Object Navigation
platform: custom Mecanum-wheeled robot (quantitative trials); Unitree Go2 quadruped and Unitree G1 humanoid (qualitative trials only)

summary_result: Real-world hard ObjectNav on the Mecanum robot: SR 98.3% versus 37.2% for InstructNav and 25.6% for VLFM, under shared sensing and low-level stack.
summary_limitation: The authors state that SysNav targets structured indoor environments and relies on room-level structure, so it may fail outdoors.

title: TARIC: Memory-Augmented Traversability-Aware Outdoor VLN Under Interrupted Semantic Cues
platform: AgileX Scout Mini (quantitative real-world trials; drive type not recorded in the legacy card); Unitree Go1 (qualitative only); simulated agents in Unreal

summary_result: Real-world Scout Mini, 40 episodes on two campus routes: combined SR 40.0% versus 17.5% for the strongest baseline (GPT-4o-GeNie).
summary_limitation: The authors report takeovers caused by pedestrians and other moving agents, memory drift over long cue-free stretches, and traversability misjudgments that cause detours.

title: From Obstacles to Etiquette: Robot Social Navigation With VLM-Informed Path Selection
platform: Boston Dynamics Spot
sensors: ELP fisheye RGB camera, Hesai JT16 mechanical LiDAR, Spot native odometry
compute: Jetson Orin onboard for navigation excluding the VLM; fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B served on an H100; end-to-end latency not reported
summary_result: Over four staged Spot scenarios with 3 trials per method, the method has zero social-zone intrusion in all four and personal-space violation 0 s in three (0.33 s queueing).
summary_limitation: The authors list three failure types: no memory beyond the current frame, ambiguous intent in concurrent activities, and post-processing that may exclude the ideal path.

title: CAUSALNAV: A Long-Term Embodied Navigation System for Autonomous Mobile Robots in Dynamic Outdoor Scenarios
platform: Agilex HUNTER SE four-wheeled robot (label in Fig. 5; drive type not recorded in the legacy card); simulated ground robot in Gazebo
sensors: RealSense D435i RGB camera, RoboSense Helios LiDAR, RTK GNSS/INS
